clue.text: Short walk? Certainly, dear

indicators.note: something cut short loses its tail, so the word for a walk drops its final letter

blocks.note: to tread is to walk
'sure!' is an emphatic yes

explanation.surface: A brief stroll is happily agreed to, with an affectionate 'dear' tacked on.
explanation.definitionFit: A treasure is a much-loved person, so the word works as an endearment like 'darling'.

clue.text: Get to do this on a golf course?

definitions.text: do this on a golf course

blocks.note: first meaning: to irritate or annoy someone

blocks.clueFragment: do this on a golf course
blocks.note: second meaning: to play the opening stroke of a hole

explanation.walkthrough: The question reads as one idea about golf, but 'Get to' is a separate meaning: to annoy, as in being 'teed off'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to make someone angry and to strike the first shot from the tee.

clue.text: Former lover criticised, by the sound of it, getting flesh out

indicators.note: this phrase says the solver should go by how the words are spoken, not spelt

blocks.note: an ex is a former lover; panned means harshly criticised

explanation.surface: A jilted partner's ex is slated, and somehow ends up putting on weight.
explanation.definitionFit: To flesh out an idea is to develop it in more detail, to enlarge on it.

clue.text: Catches small horses

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
nags are old or poor horses

explanation.surface: Someone is rounding up ponies.
explanation.definitionFit: Snags are hitches or drawbacks, much as catches are hidden problems in a deal.

clue.text: Classifying administered by Charles?

blocks.note: to run a business is to administer it
Charles III is the British king

explanation.surface: Asks whether a system of classification was overseen by King Charles.
explanation.definitionFit: Ranking things means placing them in order or grades, which is a way of sorting them.

clue.text: Fruit bats last to leave

indicators.note: the final letter is told to go, so the word is cut at its end

blocks.note: bats, like bananas, is slang for crazy

explanation.surface: Fruit bats are the final creatures to depart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fruit bats' reads as the animal, but 'bats' is the adjective meaning mad.
explanation.definitionFit: A banana is a common tropical fruit, so it is an example of the general word.

clue.text: Acknowledgement from District Attorney over delegation

indicators.note: in a down clue, turned over means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: DA is the usual US abbreviation
a mission is a group sent to represent others

explanation.surface: A prosecutor offers some recognition to a visiting delegation.
explanation.definitionFit: An admission is a confession or concession, an acknowledgement that something is true.

clue.text: Upset I get data mixed up

indicators.note: things mixed up are jumbled out of their order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone frets that their information has been scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: Agitated and upset both describe being troubled or flustered.

clue.text: Story one acted out

indicators.note: acted out suggests the letters are put into a new performance, broken from their order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A tale that one person performed in front of others.
explanation.definitionFit: An anecdote is a short amusing or personal tale, a kind of story.

clue.text: Describes six planes nearly up in the air

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
things thrown up in the air come down in a different arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
the word loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A commentator talks through a flypast of six aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: To explain something is to set it out or describe it clearly.

clue.text: Match official's sign of hesitation before quiet rage

indicators.note: before tells us which piece comes first in the line

blocks.note: um is what people say when hesitating
p is piano, the musical marking for soft
ire is anger

explanation.surface: A referee pauses, then quietly seethes.
explanation.definitionFit: An umpire is a referee who rules on play in cricket or tennis matches.

clue.text: Silver uniform with initially excellent fit

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the next word

blocks.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
U is uniform in the NATO alphabet
the first letter

explanation.surface: A silver outfit that is cut very well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit' looks like it describes how the uniform sits, but it is a noun: a bout of illness.
explanation.definitionFit: An ague is a feverish attack of shivering, a fit in the sense of a sudden bout.

clue.text: Searching around Northern Ireland is exhausting

indicators.note: around says one word wraps itself about the other

blocks.note: fishing for something is searching for it
NI is the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Hunting all over Northern Ireland wears you out.
explanation.definitionFit: A finishing day is one that finishes you off, i.e. tires you out completely.

clue.text: Half of bust plus stomach

indicators.note: half of a four-letter word keeps two of its letters, here the back pair

blocks.note: the second half of the word
and means plus

explanation.surface: Sounds like a body measurement: chest and midriff.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stomach' looks like a body part beside 'bust', but it is a verb: to put up with.
explanation.definitionFit: To stand something, as in 'I can't stand it', is to tolerate it, the verb sense of stomach.

clue.text: Joke entertaining new crowd

indicators.note: to entertain guests is to hold them within, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: a gag is a joke
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A comedian's quip amuses a fresh audience.
explanation.definitionFit: A gang is a band or group of people, a crowd in the informal sense.

clue.text: PM following leaders of nations out of necessity

indicators.note: the leaders of a set of words are their front letters

blocks.note: after means following
the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister succeeds world leaders because circumstances force it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PM' wants to be the Prime Minister; it is post meridiem, the hours after midday.
explanation.definitionFit: PM, post meridiem, marks the time after midday, which is when afternoon falls.

clue.text: Obvious I've returned with depression

indicators.note: something returned goes back the way it came, so these letters are read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe dropped
a dent is a hollow or depression in a surface

explanation.surface: Plainly, someone has come home feeling low.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' suggests low mood; here it is a physical hollow.
explanation.definitionFit: Evident and obvious both mean plain to see or clearly apparent.

clue.text: See lambs frantically flock together

indicators.note: acting frantically means moving wildly and out of order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Watch the lambs dash about and herd into a group.
explanation.definitionFit: To assemble is to gather in one place, as a flock of sheep does.

clue.text: Relax, Oscar – claret's put back

blocks.note: to rest is to relax
O is Oscar in the NATO alphabet
claret is a red wine from Bordeaux

explanation.surface: A friend called Oscar is told to unwind because the wine has been put away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put back' might suggest drinking the claret; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something restored has been returned to its former place or condition.

clue.text: Jumper a sewer fixed? About time!

indicators.note: something fixed has been repaired and set into a new working order
about means surrounding, so the remaining letters wrap round the single one

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A knitted top was finally mended by someone who sews.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a jumper is a knitted pullover, not a pinafore dress.
explanation.definitionFit: Jumper is the British word for a knitted pullover, the same garment as a sweater.

clue.text: Wander around river with nothing on in the morning

indicators.note: in a down clue, one thing on another sits above it, fixing the order

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for river
O looks like zero
am is ante meridiem, before noon

explanation.surface: Someone strolls naked by a river at dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With nothing on' suggests nudity; 'nothing' is the letter shaped like zero, placed above the morning.
explanation.definitionFit: To roam is to travel aimlessly, to stray or drift about.

clue.text: Discover female is nude on a regular basis

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

blocks.note: F is the abbreviation for female
the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Learning that a woman habitually goes without clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: To find something is to come upon it or discover it.

clue.text: Smack student in act of clemency

indicators.note: in places one piece within the other

blocks.note: a favour is a kindness or act of grace
L is a learner, as on a British learner-driver plate

explanation.surface: A pupil escapes being hit thanks to a teacher's mercy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smack' reads as a slap; it is a noun meaning a trace of taste, as in 'a smack of garlic'.
explanation.definitionFit: A smack is a characteristic taste or tinge, so it means the same as savour or taste.

clue.text: Young child at home following social worker

blocks.note: in means at home
f. is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
the ant is a social insect and a worker

explanation.surface: A toddler is home while a council welfare officer is on the case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Social worker' suggests a welfare officer; in crosswords it is often the ant, which lives in colonies.
explanation.definitionFit: An infant is a baby or very young child.

clue.text: Rubbish idea almost upset my boss

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the last letter goes
in a down clue, set upside down means read from bottom to top

blocks.note: rot is nonsense
the word without its final letter

explanation.surface: A worker grumbles that a silly suggestion has annoyed their superior.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is from the setter's point of view: a crossword compiler answers to the newspaper's puzzle chief.
explanation.definitionFit: A crossword setter's work is commissioned and checked by the newspaper's editor, so the setter's own boss.

clue.text: Set foot in two hospital departments

blocks.note: ENT is ear, nose and throat; ER is the emergency room

explanation.surface: Someone visits two wards of a hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: To set foot in a place is to go into it.

clue.text: Left one day after a party

indicators.note: after places the later pair behind the earlier ones in the line

blocks.note: taken as written
a band is a group or party of people
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: Someone departed the day after a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like a verb of departing; it is an adjective meaning deserted.
explanation.definitionFit: Something abandoned has been left behind or deserted.

clue.text: Preparing fashionable pet clothes

indicators.note: to clothe something is to cover it, so one piece wraps the other

blocks.note: a dog is a common pet
in means in fashion

explanation.surface: Dressing a pet in trendy outfits.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing a meal or a room means getting it ready, so the word can mean preparing.

clue.text: Hilltop covering ancient city's tunnel

indicators.note: a cover goes round what it protects, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: the brow of a hill is its top
Ur was a city of ancient Mesopotamia

explanation.surface: A hill crest buried an ancient city's underground passage.
explanation.definitionFit: A burrow is a hole or tunnel dug by an animal such as a rabbit.

clue.text: Controlling man I don't fancy

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or ornamental, so the letters are dressed up in a new order

blocks.note: the letters to rearrange, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone says they aren't attracted to a bossy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as the British verb for being attracted to someone, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Dominant means having power or influence over others.

clue.text: Winding up boyfriend in general? Only partly

indicators.note: only partly means just a portion of the words is used, a run of letters inside them

blocks.note: the run of letters across the word gap

explanation.surface: Asks whether someone is teasing boyfriends as a class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winding up' reads as teasing; it means bringing to a close.
explanation.definitionFit: Winding up something means bringing it to a conclusion, its close.

clue.text: More intelligent, annoying person changing direction inside?

indicators.note: one compass-style side, left, swaps for the other, right, within the word

blocks.note: a blighter is a British word for an irritating person

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a pest is smarter for an inner change of course.
explanation.walkthrough: L (left) becomes R (right) inside the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Bright means clever, so the comparative means cleverer.
